whyCorrect: The blank has to name the change the vacuum pan produces, and the text tells you exactly what that change is: at ordinary pressure the syrup scorches, but under vacuum it boils at a far lower temperature so nothing darkens. Lowering the temperature of a hard boil is what makes it gentle. Read the sentence before the blank and look for the word that renames the effect already described.

whyWrong.B: Nothing in the text says the vacuum boil is quicker; the stated benefit is that the syrup is not scorched, which is about heat, not speed.
whyWrong.C: Cost never appears in the text. A vacuum pan is expensive equipment, so this is an assumption you bring from outside rather than something the passage supports.
whyWrong.D: The boil still happens under vacuum — water is still driven off until crystals appear. The vacuum changes the conditions of the boil, it does not remove the need for one.

commonMistakes: Choosing a word that sounds like an industrial advantage in general rather than the one advantage the text actually describes.
tips: In a word-in-context item, the correct word is usually a one-word summary of a phrase already in the passage.

whyCorrect: Sugar leaves the cells because the liquid outside is weaker than the liquid inside — that gap is what drives the movement. Because each vessel supplies water even poorer in sugar than the last, the gap is restored at every stage instead of shrinking to nothing. Renewed names that repeated restoration.

whyWrong.A: The passage describes what makes the sugar move, not any act of measuring it; no gauge or reading is mentioned.
whyWrong.B: Nothing reverses. The sugar travels in one direction the whole way, out of the cossettes and into the water.
whyWrong.D: Reduced is the opposite of what the countercurrent arrangement achieves — fresher water at each stage keeps the difference large rather than letting it fall.

commonMistakes: Confusing the sugar concentration (which does fall from vessel to vessel) with the difference in concentration, which is the thing kept up.

whyCorrect: The semicolon sets up a contrast with "never travels through the air," so the blank must name spread by contact. The text describes workers licking the blend off the queen and passing it on as they groom one another — one bee to the next, in a chain. Relayed is exactly that hand-to-hand transfer.

whyWrong.B: Broadcast means sent out in all directions at once, which is the airborne spread the sentence explicitly rules out.
whyWrong.C: The compound is not hidden; the whole point is that thirty thousand bees register it within an hour.
whyWrong.D: Dilution would explain a weakening signal, but the text is describing how the message reaches every bee, not how strong it stays.

tips: When a sentence contains a "not X; it is _____" structure, the blank must contrast with X.

whyCorrect: The clause after the comma gives the reason: every part of the coat is a live bee. So the coat is not a structure the colony assembles out of materials — the bees themselves are its substance. Constitutes means makes up or forms, which is the relationship the reason clause requires.

whyWrong.A: Nothing is hidden. The outer bees are in plain view acting as insulation.
whyWrong.B: To occupy a coat is to be inside something separate from you; the point is that there is no separate coat for the bees to sit in.
whyWrong.D: Imports would mean bringing the coat in from elsewhere, but the bees supplying the insulation are the colony's own.

commonMistakes: Reading "not something the colony builds" as a hint that the coat came from outside, rather than that the bees are the coat.

whyCorrect: The last sentence concedes that sugar is still in the liquor, so the blank cannot claim the sugar is gone. What the repeated boiling and spinning has done is take out everything worth taking — further work would cost more than it returns. Exhausted carries exactly that sense of worked as far as it pays to work.

whyWrong.A: Concentrated describes the syrup at every earlier stage too, so it fails to capture what makes this liquor final.
whyWrong.C: Purified is backwards: the syrup gets darker and dirtier each time crystals are removed, not cleaner.
whyWrong.D: Wasted would contradict the passage, which explains that the syrup was worked repeatedly until further work stopped paying.

tips: When a sentence begins "not X; it is simply _____," the blank must be compatible with X being partly true.

whyCorrect: The text is built around one turn: the soil deduction "looks like an accountant's nicety," and then "but" introduces the figures that show it is not — a fifth of a load can be soil, and the factory would pay to haul and wash it. The purpose is to overturn the impression that the deduction is trivial. Locate the pivot word and the purpose usually follows from it.

whyWrong.B: The text defends the charge rather than calling it unfair; it explains what the factory would otherwise be paying for.
whyWrong.C: The weighbridge and sampling are mentioned only as setup. A description of equipment would not need the "but" clause that carries the point.
whyWrong.D: A wet season is named only to show how large the tare can get; there is no dry season in the text to compare it with.

whyCorrect: The last sentence tells you what the text is for: the freeze-killed brood test "says nothing about the disease itself, only about the colony's housekeeping, and it is the housekeeping that is passed on." So the text explains how a breeder can score an inherited behaviour using dead brood rather than infected brood. The whole middle of the passage is the method, and the final clause is why it works.

whyWrong.B: No symptoms are given. The only sign described — a dead larva sealed in its cell — is the starting condition, not a diagnostic list.
whyWrong.C: Liquid nitrogen appears as a tool for killing a patch of brood; no hazard is mentioned anywhere.
whyWrong.D: Only one disease is discussed, so there is nothing being compared.

whyCorrect: Track the arc of the passage: the industry was built for a wartime reason (the blockade), it failed commercially once the blockade lifted, but the varieties and plant survived for a later revival. A main-idea choice has to include the whole arc, and only this one keeps both the failure and what outlived it. A choice covering just one sentence is a detail, not the main idea.

whyWrong.B: The blockade's effect on price is the background in the first sentence, not what the text is about.
whyWrong.C: This contradicts the text, which says the industry could not compete and much of it failed.
whyWrong.D: The text never claims beet displaced cane; it says the beet industry failed and was revived a generation later.

whyCorrect: The question asks for a stated reason, so find the word "because" in the text: dressings are irradiated "because the spores of certain soil organisms survive what kills everything else." Honey's low water and its peroxide destroy ordinary bacteria, but those spores get through, so an extra step is needed. This choice restates that sentence without adding anything.

whyWrong.A: Irradiation is used to kill surviving spores; the text never links it to peroxide levels.
whyWrong.B: The text says nothing about honey gaining water once it is packed, and if it did, that would not be what irradiation addresses.
whyWrong.C: This reverses the first sentence, which says bacteria placed in honey die.

tips: For an "according to the text" question, find the sentence that answers it and pick the choice that paraphrases only that sentence.

whyCorrect: The expectation to be borne out is that more glucose means faster setting, so the completion needs two sources whose glucose and setting time move in opposite directions. Oilseed rape at 40 per cent set in 2 weeks and ling heather at 28 per cent took 26 weeks — the highest glucose with the shortest time, the lowest with the longest. A single reading cannot show a relationship between two variables.

whyWrong.A: This gives lime's glucose but no setting time, so it shows no relationship at all.
whyWrong.B: True from the table, but it reports only setting times; without the glucose figures it cannot support a claim about glucose.
whyWrong.D: Clover's 9 weeks is accurate but stands alone, and one source's setting time demonstrates nothing about the effect of glucose.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice just because its numbers match the table. Accuracy is not enough — the data cited has to include both variables the claim connects.

whyCorrect: The claim is that the thermometer reading reflects the water still in the syrup rather than the heat that has gone in. To support it you want a case where the heat history differs but the reading tracks the water anyway. Two syrups with the same water content boiling at the same temperature — one driven hard, one brought up slowly — separates the two explanations and leaves only water content standing.

whyWrong.A: This links final hardness to temperature, which both explanations already predict; it does not distinguish water content from heat input.
whyWrong.B: The cold-water ball test is an alternative to a thermometer, so it says nothing about what the thermometer reading measures.
whyWrong.D: A wide pan reaching a temperature sooner is about the rate of evaporation, not about what the temperature reading corresponds to.

tips: To test a claim of the form "X really measures P, not Q," look for evidence where Q varies and the reading does not.

whyCorrect: The text describes two things happening together as lifting is delayed: sugar goes up and soil tare goes up. "Both halves of this pattern" means the completion must report both trends. From 20 September to 5 December the sugar rose 15.8 to 18.2 per cent and the tare rose 6 to 21 per cent, which is the only choice giving both.

whyWrong.B: One sugar reading on one date shows neither trend.
whyWrong.C: This covers the soil tare only, leaving the sugar half of the pattern unreported.
whyWrong.D: The sugar did rise across the dates, but the claim still omits the soil tare entirely, and "rose on every one of the four dates" misdescribes a table whose first date is a starting point, not a rise.

commonMistakes: Answering with one accurate number when the sentence has promised two related trends.

whyCorrect: The passage gives the mechanism: beet flowers only after a spell of cold, and a plant meeting a cold April bolts, sending its sugar into a seed stem instead of the root. Sowing earlier puts young plants into exactly that cold spell growers are waiting out. The completion has to name the consequence the stated mechanism produces, not any general risk of early sowing.

whyWrong.A: Drought is never mentioned, and an earlier-sown crop would be further along by midsummer if anything.
whyWrong.B: Germination rate is not discussed; the passage's concern is bolting in plants that do come up.
whyWrong.D: This is the risk of sowing too late, not too early; earlier sowing gives the root more season, not less.

whyCorrect: Work backwards from the two signs. Several eggs per cell is how an unmated worker lays, and drone brood in worker-sized cells means the eggs were unfertilised — both are the signature of laying workers. The text says laying workers appear only after a colony has been queenless for a few weeks with no young larvae to raise a new queen, so that is what the beekeeper can conclude.

whyWrong.B: A poorly laying queen would still lay one egg per cell and would still lay fertilised eggs, so neither sign fits.
whyWrong.C: Where a queen mated is irrelevant; the signs point to eggs laid by unmated workers, not by any queen.
whyWrong.D: Royal jelly feeding is what produces a queen, and the passage says this colony has no queen and no larvae from which to raise one.

tips: Inference completions must stay inside the mechanism the text supplies — do not add a cause the passage never mentions.

whyCorrect: "a Presbyterian minister in Philadelphia" is a nonrestrictive appositive renaming Lorenzo Langstroth, and the comma after "Philadelphia" closes it. A nonrestrictive appositive has to be fenced on both sides with the same mark, so the blank needs the opening comma. Check for a closing comma later in the sentence — it tells you an opening one is required.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon joins two independent clauses. "a Presbyterian minister in Philadelphia" has no verb and is not a clause.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation the appositive is left open at the front while still being closed at the back, so the fencing is unmatched.
whyWrong.D: A colon must follow a complete independent clause; "Lorenzo Langstroth" alone is only a subject.

tips: Half a pair of commas is always wrong — look for the mark on the other side of the phrase.

whyCorrect: "which replaced the older presses in the 1870s" is a nonrestrictive relative clause, and the comma after "1870s" closes it. Such a clause must be set off with a comma at each end, so the blank takes the opening comma. A which clause in Standard English is nearly always nonrestrictive and punctuated this way.

whyWrong.A: Leaving the blank bare closes the clause without opening it, which strands the comma after "1870s".
whyWrong.B: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides; a relative clause beginning with "which" is not independent.
whyWrong.C: A colon must be preceded by a complete independent clause, and "The diffusion battery" is only a noun phrase.

whyCorrect: "Bees do not gather honeydew from flowers" and "they gather it from the sticky drops aphids leave on leaves" are both complete independent clauses, and no coordinating conjunction joins them. A semicolon is the mark that links two independent clauses without a conjunction. Test each side for a subject and a verb before choosing punctuation.

whyWrong.A: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: With no mark at all the two clauses run together as a fused sentence.
whyWrong.C: A colon introduces an explanation or a list that the first clause has set up; here the second clause corrects the first rather than unpacking a promise made by it.

commonMistakes: Assuming a comma is enough because the two clauses are short and closely related.

whyCorrect: "A boiled sweet asks three things of the syrup it is made from" is a complete independent clause that announces a list, and the three items follow. A colon is the mark that introduces a list after a complete clause. The word "three" in the clause is the signal that an enumeration is coming.

whyWrong.B: A comma cannot introduce a list of items that themselves contain commas, and it fails to mark the break between the announcement and the enumeration.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides; what follows is a series of noun phrases, not a clause.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation, "made from enough acid" reads as a single phrase and the list structure disappears.

whyCorrect: "Opened in cold weather" is a participial phrase, and the noun immediately after the comma must be the thing that was opened. Only a hive can be opened, so "a hive" has to be the subject of the main clause. This is the modifier-attachment rule: put the modified noun first, or the modifier dangles.

whyWrong.A: This makes "beekeepers" the thing opened in cold weather.
whyWrong.B: The subject is the empty "it" of "it is a mistake," so nothing in the clause is available for the participle to modify.
whyWrong.D: This makes "the colony" the thing opened, but it is the hive that gets opened; the colony is what is inside it.

tips: With an opening participial phrase, read the first noun after the comma and ask whether it can perform or receive that action.

whyCorrect: The sentence lists what the day was spent doing: "boiling syrup, pulling it over a hook … and _____ it into ropes." Items in a series must take the same grammatical form, and the first two are -ing participles, so the third must be "drawing." Parallel structure is decided by the other items in the list, not by the sentence's main verb.

whyWrong.A: "drew" is a past-tense verb, which breaks the series of participles and leaves the sentence with two competing main verbs.
whyWrong.B: An infinitive does not match "boiling" and "pulling."
whyWrong.C: "draws" is a present-tense finite verb, wrong in both form and tense for a list of participles.

whyCorrect: With "neither … nor," the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. That subject is "the old queen," which is singular, so the singular "shows" is required. The plural "workers" sits in the first half of the pair and does not control the verb.

whyWrong.B: "show" is the plural form, agreeing with "workers" rather than with the nearer subject "the old queen."
whyWrong.C: "have shown" is plural and also shifts to the present perfect, which clashes with the simple past narration of the sentence.
whyWrong.D: "are showing" is plural, and the progressive does not match the sentence's description of a state over weeks.

tips: For neither/nor and either/or subjects, match the verb to whichever subject stands closest to it.

whyCorrect: The second sentence does not add new information; it restates the first in different terms. "Comes from the flowers the colony actually worked, not from whatever the beekeeper planted" and "records the bees' choices rather than the choices offered to them" are the same point twice. A restatement transition is what the relationship calls for.

whyWrong.A: An example would have to be a specific instance of the first sentence's claim, but the second sentence is a general restatement.
whyWrong.B: "Earlier" signals a shift back in time, and neither sentence is about a sequence of events.
whyWrong.D: "Nevertheless" marks a contrast, yet the two sentences agree completely.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives a cause: an upright wick chars into a stub and blocks the wax climbing behind it. The second gives the consequence for the candle owner — frequent trimming to stop it smoking. A result transition is what links a cause to its effect.

whyWrong.B: There is no opposition between the two sentences; the second follows from the first.
whyWrong.C: The second sentence is not an instance of a charring wick — it is what the charring makes necessary.
whyWrong.D: "Admittedly" concedes a point against the writer's argument, and nothing here is being conceded.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says honey never spoils; the second says an open jar takes up water until yeasts can work in it — spoilage. That is a limitation on the first claim, so the transition must signal contrast. "Even so" concedes the first statement while introducing the exception.

whyWrong.A: "Similarly" claims the two sentences make the same point, but one says honey keeps and the other says it ferments.
whyWrong.B: "In short" introduces a summary, and the second sentence adds a new condition rather than summarising.
whyWrong.D: "Accordingly" makes the spoilage a consequence of never spoiling, which reverses the logic.

whyCorrect: The goal names two things that must both appear: the discovery, and the hand labour it removed. Only this choice carries the cluster seed, the singling it forced, the 1948 single-fruit plant, and the drilling that replaced the hand work — the full chain from problem to solution. Match a synthesis answer against the stated goal, not against how much of the note list it copies.

whyWrong.A: This defines singling but never mentions the discovery, so nothing is shown to have been removed.
whyWrong.B: This reports the discovery with no indication of what labour it did away with.
whyWrong.D: This gives only the botanical starting point, leaving out both the labour and the discovery.

tips: When the goal joins two ideas with "how X did Y," the right choice has to contain both X and Y.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain how the board empties a super, so the answer needs the mechanism: where the board goes, that the escape is one-way, that the bees drift down and cannot return, and the result by morning. Only this choice supplies the whole sequence. The other three each state one isolated fact from the notes.

whyWrong.A: This gives the outcome but not the mechanism the goal asks you to explain.
whyWrong.C: This restates the problem the board solves rather than how it solves it.
whyWrong.D: The one-way escape is the key part, but on its own it does not explain how the super ends up empty.

whyCorrect: The goal is to justify a rule with two acceptable extremes, so the answer must explain both the short move and the long one and say why the middle fails. This choice gives the cause — foragers return to a remembered position — then the under-a-metre case, the over-three-kilometre case, and the clustering that happens in between. A single note cannot cover a rule with two branches.

whyWrong.A: This shows only what goes wrong in the middle range, with neither safe distance explained.
whyWrong.B: This covers the long move alone, so the short move is left unjustified.
whyWrong.D: Orientation flights are background; they do not state the rule or either of its two branches.

whyCorrect: The passage says crystallisation is inevitable and that the packer "does not fight this." Seeding with fine crystals does not stop the change; it decides how the change happens, giving thousands of small starting points so no crystal grows coarse. Govern names that control over the form the change takes.

whyWrong.B: Seeding speeds the set up rather than putting it off — the crystals are supplied deliberately.
whyWrong.C: Nothing is undone. The glucose still comes out of solution; only the crystal size differs.
whyWrong.D: The set is visible and intended; a smooth set is the product being sold, not a change being hidden.

tips: "Not X so much as _____" needs a word that contrasts with X while still fitting what the passage described.

whyCorrect: The text rules out any deciding individual: no bee compares sites, and a site wins once the number of inspectors gathered there passes a threshold. The decision is therefore the sum of many separate arrivals building up over time. Accumulated is the word for a result reached by adding up rather than by choosing.

whyWrong.A: Rehearsed suggests practice beforehand, but the dances recruit inspectors in real time and settle the outcome as they go.
whyWrong.C: Imposed requires someone with authority to impose it, which the sentence explicitly denies.
whyWrong.D: Inherited would make the choice of site something passed down, whereas each swarm arrives at its own by counting.

whyCorrect: Everything in the passage is about crystals: the sweet is a syrup cooled so fast that molecules never line up, pure sucrose grains within weeks, and the acid splits sucrose into sugars that block the lattice. The property being preserved is the glassy, uncrystallised state. Clear is the word for a sweet that has not gone grainy and opaque.

whyWrong.A: Splitting sucrose is described as a way to obstruct crystals, and the text never raises sweetness as the aim.
whyWrong.B: Hardness in a boiled sweet comes from low moisture, which the passage does not connect to the acid.
whyWrong.C: Cost never enters the passage.

commonMistakes: Choosing a general-sounding quality of a boiled sweet instead of the specific problem — graining — that the acid is added to prevent.

whyCorrect: The yellow light is solid carbon, and the text follows that carbon to the outer edge "where the air arrives." Carbon meeting oxygen at high temperature is consumed, so "spent" here means burned away. Substitute each option into the sentence and keep the one that fits carbon meeting air in a flame.

whyWrong.B: This is the financial sense of the word; nothing in the passage involves payment.
whyWrong.C: Exhausted by effort applies to a living thing that has tired, not to a particle of carbon.
whyWrong.D: Scattering would move the carbon outward without consuming it, but the point of the outer edge is that oxygen reaches it there.

whyCorrect: The charred bone holds the coloured molecules on its surface while the sugar passes on through, so the bed catches the colour on its way and lets the rest continue. Intercepts is precisely that catching of something in transit. The sentence also insists the sugar itself is unchanged, so the word must describe an action on the colour alone.

whyWrong.A: Dissolving would put the coloured compounds into solution, but they were already in solution and are being taken out of it.
whyWrong.B: The passage stresses that the bed "changes nothing about the sugar," so it cannot be altering taste.
whyWrong.C: Nothing is increased; the whole purpose is removal.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes that density rises with sugar content, and the underlined sentence draws the practical consequence: print the stem in per cent sugar instead of density. The next sentence confirms the effect — the boiler reads the figure straight off and calculates nothing. Its job is to bridge the physical fact and the number the user wants.

whyWrong.A: Why a hydrometer floats is never explained anywhere in the text; only how far it floats is used.
whyWrong.C: The limitation arrives in the final clause about other dissolved substances, and nothing withdraws it.
whyWrong.D: No particular syrup is named, so nothing here functions as an example.

whyCorrect: The sentence before gives the measurement — bees leave a clear gap of about eight millimetres — and the underlined sentence puts it to work by spacing the frames at that width. The sentence after gives the payoff: comb attached only to the frame, so the hive opens without damage. The underlined sentence is the hinge between the finding and the result.

whyWrong.A: Nothing casts doubt on the measurement; the text uses it as established fact.
whyWrong.B: The difficulty was stated at the start, with comb having to be cut out; this sentence is part of the solution.
whyWrong.C: No contemporary's hive is described, so no comparison is made.

whyCorrect: The text holds two things together: what is settled (queens meet drones from other colonies, which is the point of the arrangement) and what is not (how each generation finds sites no living drone has visited). A main-idea answer has to keep both. Watch for the sentences "What draws them there is still argued over" and "What is clear is …" — they mark the two halves.

whyWrong.A: The landscape fold is mentioned as an association, and the text explicitly says the cause is still argued over.
whyWrong.C: The text says no drone lives long enough to have visited a site in a previous season, so memory is ruled out.
whyWrong.D: This reverses the closing sentence, which says the queen meets drones from colonies other than her own.

whyCorrect: The final sentence names the limit directly: the method fails whenever other optically active substances are present, and beet molasses contains several. Optically active means they rotate polarised light too, so their rotation is added to the sucrose's and the reading no longer reports sucrose alone.

whyWrong.A: The text says the opposite — the polarisation figure is what contracts print.
whyWrong.B: Molasses is said to contain other active substances besides sucrose, not to be free of sucrose.
whyWrong.D: Proportionality is stated as the principle the instrument rests on, not as the thing that fails.

whyCorrect: The student's claim is about the timetable, not the scale of the plant, so the quotation must be about time. This one runs from the first slice in September to the last in January and adds that the crews worked in eight-hour turns without the diffusers ever stopping — continuous operation stated twice over. The other three all measure the factory in metres or tonnes.

whyWrong.A: Four storeys high is a statement of size, which is the emphasis the student is arguing against.
whyWrong.C: The length of the evaporator hall is again scale, not schedule.
whyWrong.D: Twelve thousand tonnes in the yard measures how much the plant holds, not how continuously it runs.

tips: Read the claim for the word that must appear in the evidence — here it is time, not size.

whyCorrect: The scholar's claim is that Verrell treats the hive as a workplace to be managed. This quotation is pure management: a sequence of instructions, an eye on the clock, and a cost stated in what the colony loses. Look for imperative verbs and practical consequences when a claim is about a practical stance.

whyWrong.A: Standing in the orchard letting the work wait is admiration overriding management — the opposite of the claim.
whyWrong.B: This is lyrical generalisation about the bee's year, with nothing being managed.
whyWrong.C: A family detail about where hives stood shows tradition, not a managerial attitude.

whyCorrect: The proposal has to be separated from its rival: heat generated by the bees versus heat retained by the cavity. Colonies in thin-walled hives holding the same centre temperature as insulated ones show that insulation is not what sets the temperature, and the extra stores eaten show the bees are paying for the heat with fuel they burn themselves. That is both halves of the proposal.

whyWrong.A: More stores meaning better survival is consistent with either explanation and says nothing about where the heat comes from.
whyWrong.C: A centre temperature that tracks the outside temperature would if anything weaken the claim that the bees hold it up themselves.
whyWrong.D: A warm centre and cool edge is just the temperature gradient already described in the passage, not evidence about its source.

whyCorrect: The text gives two things that raise HMF: time in storage and warmth. A blend near the ceiling therefore has a history of one or both in at least one of its components. Since only these two causes have been supplied, the conclusion has to be limited to them.

whyWrong.A: The packer's measurement says nothing about whether the legal limit is set well; that is a judgement the text gives no basis for.
whyWrong.C: Added syrup is never linked to HMF anywhere in the passage.
whyWrong.D: Sealing of the comb is not mentioned, and fresh honey is said to contain no HMF regardless.

commonMistakes: Jumping to adulteration. A high HMF reading is evidence of heat or age, which is all the passage connects it to.

whyCorrect: The passage supplies one mechanism that stops yeast: too little free water. It also says the more freely the honey is diluted, the more readily the ferment runs. A ferment that stalls with plenty of sugar left is the case where the yeast has run out of water rather than fuel, so insufficient dilution is the first thing to suspect.

whyWrong.A: An open vessel is not connected to a stall anywhere in the text; if anything it lets more water in.
whyWrong.C: Honey's sugar does not disappear with age — the passage says a sealed jar keeps for years.
whyWrong.D: This contradicts the premise, which states a great deal of sugar is still unfermented.

whyCorrect: "Because wax scales form only while a bee is young and generously fed" is a subordinate clause opening the sentence, and the main clause "a colony … cannot draw new comb" follows it. A dependent clause placed before its main clause is separated from it by a comma. Find the subordinating word — here "Because" — and the punctuation follows automatically.

whyWrong.B: With nothing at the boundary, "fed a colony" runs together and the reader loses where the subordinate clause ends.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and a "Because" clause is dependent.
whyWrong.D: A colon must be preceded by an independent clause, which a "Because" clause is not.

whyCorrect: "A swarm … will die within a few days if it finds nowhere to live" and "The scouts that leave it are looking for a dry cavity" are both complete sentences with no conjunction between them. A period is the mark that separates two independent clauses here. Test the second half for a subject and verb: "scouts … are looking" is a full clause.

whyWrong.A: This fuses the two clauses with no punctuation at all.
whyWrong.B: A colon is not used before a coordinating conjunction, and "and" is unnecessary once the clauses are separated.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two independent clauses without a conjunction is a comma splice.

whyCorrect: "spins the massecuite" and "washes the crystals" are two verbs sharing the single subject "A refiner," so this is a compound predicate rather than two clauses. A compound predicate joined by "and" takes no punctuation before the conjunction. Check whether a subject appears after "and" — none does here.

whyWrong.A: A colon would announce a list or explanation, and what follows is simply the refiner's second action.
whyWrong.C: A comma before "and" is used when the conjunction joins two independent clauses, but "washes the crystals" has no subject of its own.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides.

commonMistakes: Adding a comma before every "and" — it belongs there only when a full clause follows.

whyCorrect: Both halves are independent clauses, and "consequently" is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction — it cannot join clauses on its own. The convention is a semicolon before it and a comma after. Words like consequently, however and therefore always take this treatment between two full clauses.

whyWrong.A: With no mark before "consequently" the two clauses are fused.
whyWrong.B: A colon signals that what follows explains or lists, and it is not the mark used ahead of a conjunctive adverb linking two clauses.
whyWrong.D: A comma before "consequently" leaves two independent clauses joined by a comma, which is a splice.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets two past events in order: nobody found a method, and then Achard opened his factory half a century later. The earlier of two completed past events takes the past perfect, so "had found" is required. The clue is the "until …" clause, which supplies the later past reference point.

whyWrong.A: "finds" is present tense and contradicts the 1747 setting.
whyWrong.B: "will find" places the search in the future, which cannot be right for something ended by an event in the past.
whyWrong.C: "is finding" is present progressive and clashes with the past-tense narration in the rest of the sentence.

whyCorrect: The subject is "A row," which is singular; "of wax moulds" is a prepositional phrase and the interrupting participial phrase between the commas is not the subject either. A singular subject takes "stands," and the present tense matches "where the light is best." Strip out everything between the subject and the verb before deciding agreement.

whyWrong.B: "stand" agrees with "moulds," a noun inside a prepositional phrase, which can never be the subject.
whyWrong.C: "have stood" is plural and shifts the tense to the present perfect.
whyWrong.D: "were standing" is plural and past, clashing with the present-tense "is best" later in the sentence.

whyCorrect: "A colony" is a singular noun, so the possessive pronoun referring to it must be the singular "its." The possessive form of it carries no apostrophe. Say the sentence with "it is" in the blank as a test — it fails, so the apostrophe form is wrong.

whyWrong.A: "their" is plural and does not agree with the singular "A colony."
whyWrong.C: "it's" is the contraction of it is, which produces "has lost it is queen."
whyWrong.D: "its'" is not a word in Standard English.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a general statement — several additions will keep syrup from graining — and the second names one of them, glucose syrup, and says how it works. Moving from a general class to one member of it calls for an exemplifying transition.

whyWrong.A: A comparison would require two things weighed against each other, but only one addition is named.
whyWrong.C: "Instead" replaces a rejected option, and nothing in the first sentence has been rejected.
whyWrong.D: "Nonetheless" marks a concession, yet the second sentence supports the first rather than qualifying it.

whyCorrect: The passage is running through a process in order — washing, weighing, slicing — and the second sentence gives the stage that follows slicing. A sequence transition is what a step-by-step description needs.

whyWrong.A: "Instead" would mean diffusion replaces the earlier steps, but they all happen.
whyWrong.B: "By contrast" sets up a difference, and no two things are being contrasted.
whyWrong.C: "Nevertheless" signals a concession, which nothing in either sentence calls for.

whyCorrect: The excluder keeps brood out of the upper boxes, and pale comb fit to sell is the direct outcome of never having brood raised in it. Cause in the first sentence, effect in the second, so the transition has to express result.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" would set the second sentence against the first, but it follows from it.
whyWrong.B: Pale comb is a consequence of the excluder, not an example of one.
whyWrong.C: "Meanwhile" places two things side by side in time, which loses the causal link the passage depends on.

whyCorrect: The goal asks how the extractor separates wax from what is mixed with it, so the answer needs heat, flow and the strainer that holds the debris back. This choice supplies all three, ending with the slumgum left behind. The other options each state one fact and leave the separation unexplained.

whyWrong.B: The purity of cappings is background about the raw material, not about separation.
whyWrong.C: This describes the apparatus without saying what it does.
whyWrong.D: Naming the residue gives the by-product without the process that produced it.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain why beekeepers narrow entrances, so the answer must give the reasoning as well as the practice. This choice links the weak colony's shortage of guards and robbing's tendency to recruit more robbers to the narrowed entrance that heads it off. A choice reporting only the practice or only one condition answers a different question.

whyWrong.A: This states the threat but never mentions the entrance or why narrowing it helps.
whyWrong.B: Guard behaviour alone does not explain the beekeeper's action.
whyWrong.C: This describes what beekeepers do without giving a single reason for it.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain why poor households chose rushlights, which requires both what a rushlight cost them — nothing but a rush and leftover fat — and what the alternatives cost. Only this choice puts the free materials and the useful hour of light next to the price of tallow and beeswax. The comparison is the explanation.

whyWrong.B: This defines a rushlight without touching on cost.
whyWrong.C: The supporting strip is a construction detail with no bearing on why the poor used them.
whyWrong.D: The price of candles is half the argument; without the rushlight's near-zero cost it explains nothing.

whyCorrect: The impurities start out dissolved and end up locked into chalk that settles to the bottom. "Fixes" is being used in its chemical sense — holding a substance in a solid, unmovable form instead of letting it stay in solution. The contrast at the end of the sentence, "what would otherwise stay in solution," tells you the word must mean the opposite of remaining free and dissolved.

whyWrong.A: Determines is the sense of fixing a value or a date; nothing in the passage settles a quantity.
whyWrong.B: Prepares would mean getting the impurities ready for something further, but they are being removed and discarded.
whyWrong.D: Repairs treats the impurities as damaged, and nothing here is being mended.

tips: For an underlined-word question, find the phrase in the same sentence that the word is set against.

whyCorrect: The sentence explains that the standard was a burning candle, so its value changed with the wax used and how the wick was trimmed. That is a value that is not constant from one measurement to the next — it varied. The word choice must fit a numerical standard, not a moving object.

whyWrong.A: Gathered means collected together, which cannot be done to the value of a standard.
whyWrong.C: Floated is the literal, physical sense of drifting and does not describe a quantity changing with conditions.
whyWrong.D: Wandering off course implies a single known destination departed from, but the point is that there was no fixed value to depart from in the first place.

whyCorrect: The passage says any female larva can become a queen and that feeding alone settles which one does. So caste is not carried in the egg — it is granted to the larva afterwards by how she is fed. Conferred is the word for a status bestowed from outside rather than possessed from the start.

whyWrong.A: Predicted would mean caste is forecast after hatching, but the passage says it is decided then, not foreseen.
whyWrong.B: Inherited means passed down in the egg, which is exactly what the sentence rules out.
whyWrong.C: Nothing is turned around; a larva does not start as one caste and switch to the other.

commonMistakes: Picking a word about knowing the caste rather than about causing it.

whyCorrect: Stirring the honey makes it fluid and leaving it alone lets it stiffen again, so the thickness changes according to what is done to it. The blank sits opposite "a fixed property," so it must name something handling does to the thickness. Altered is the word for a property that changes under treatment.

whyWrong.A: Preserved means kept unchanged, which contradicts the contrast with "fixed property."
whyWrong.C: Handling changes the honey rather than measuring it; no measurement is described.
whyWrong.D: Certified would mean formally attested, and nothing in the passage involves verification.

whyCorrect: The pollen preserves the shape of the plant that shed it, so a microscopist can read off which flowers were worked and roughly where the hive stood. That makes the pollen an unintentional account of where the honey came from. Record is the word for information preserved without anyone meaning to preserve it.

whyWrong.A: An advertisement is made deliberately to be seen, which contradicts "entirely unintended."
whyWrong.B: Flavour is never mentioned; the pollen is being read, not tasted.
whyWrong.D: A guarantee is a formal assurance issued by someone, and the pollen carries no such backing.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence denies one account of the cone shape — that it was chosen for display — and the sentence after it supplies the real one: the cone was the draining mould that let molasses run out through a hole at the point. Its function is to clear a wrong explanation out of the way. "It was" opening the next sentence is the signal that a replacement explanation is coming.

whyWrong.A: The nippers appear in the first sentence, before the underlined one, and nothing new about tools follows.
whyWrong.B: Refining is never doubted; the passage goes on to explain how the refining was done.
whyWrong.C: Only one mould is described, so no two kinds are set against each other.

whyCorrect: Every sentence marks a difference from honeybee practice: pots instead of hexagonal comb, thinner and more acid honey that will not travel, and logs opened at the end rather than at the top. The text accumulates contrasts rather than building an argument or a history. When each sentence adds another difference, the purpose is to lay those differences out.

whyWrong.A: Yucatán keepers get one sentence, and no dates or stages of a history are given.
whyWrong.B: The bees' lack of a sting is in the name only; the text never explains it.
whyWrong.D: The text says the honey travels badly and has stayed local, and it never argues that this should change.

whyCorrect: The chain in the text runs: workers build two cell sizes, the queen's egg type follows the cell she meets, so the comb itself is a record of what the workers decided. The last sentence makes the timing explicit — drone comb in June shows a decision taken weeks earlier, before any brood was in it. The main idea has to be that the comb reveals prior choices.

whyWrong.A: Frames are never mentioned as a condition of building; the beekeeper only looks at what has been built.
whyWrong.C: The workers build the cells and so set the sizes; the queen responds to the cell she finds.
whyWrong.D: The text says drone and worker cells differ in size, which is what makes the comb readable.

whyCorrect: The mechanism is a near-miss in shape: raffinose is close enough to sucrose to occupy a site at the crystal face, but different enough that the next layer cannot settle on top of it. Both halves of that similarity-and-difference are what does the damage, and only this choice keeps both.

whyWrong.A: The text says crystallisation is slowed and crystals deformed, not that none form.
whyWrong.B: This contradicts the passage, which rests on raffinose being close in shape to sucrose.
whyWrong.D: The text says raffinose is "one reason," which leaves room for others.

whyCorrect: The expectation links two variables — higher melting point, slower burning — so the completion must cite both variables for at least two waxes. Beeswax at 64 °C burning 52 minutes per centimetre against paraffin at 52 °C burning only 38 shows the highest melting point with the slowest burn and the lowest with the fastest. A single row cannot demonstrate a relationship.

whyWrong.A: This reports melting points only, with no burning times to relate them to.
whyWrong.B: Stearin's 47 minutes is accurate but gives one variable for one wax.
whyWrong.C: Beeswax having the highest melting point is true, but without its burning time it supports nothing about burning rate.

commonMistakes: Treating "the numbers are correct" as enough. The citation also has to contain both quantities the expectation connects.

whyCorrect: The claim is that pollen marks a place rather than a time of year, so the supporting evidence must show place mattering more than season. Two apiaries fifty kilometres apart differing more in the same month than one apiary differs across months does exactly that: it holds season constant and finds a bigger gap by location. Ask which variable the finding isolates.

whyWrong.A: Pollen-only plants widen the range of species recorded but say nothing about place versus season.
whyWrong.B: Durability makes the record last; it does not show what the record identifies.
whyWrong.C: Shifting flowering dates make the season harder to read, which weakens the rival explanation only indirectly and offers no evidence about place.

whyCorrect: The claim is about marks left on the maker's body, so the quotation has to describe the speaker physically. Ridged thumbs worn by the running wick, and a smell that follows the speaker home, are the trade written on the person. The other quotations describe the shop, the street or the wax.

whyWrong.B: The hanging tapers are a description of the goods, with the maker absent.
whyWrong.C: The dark street and the shutters set a scene outside the shop entirely.
whyWrong.D: Wax keeping its shape is a remark about the material, not about the chandler.

whyCorrect: The passage says the film comes from inside the wax, that warming and rubbing clears it, and — crucially — that "in time the film returns." A cure that does not last means the timing matters: the treatment has to happen shortly before the candle reaches the customer. The completion has to follow from the return of the film, which is the last fact given.

whyWrong.A: The film is stated to come from the wax's own longer-chain components, not out of the air, so sealing the box addresses nothing.
whyWrong.B: The text rules out a residue from handling by identifying the film as material migrating from within.
whyWrong.C: Nothing is spoiled; the film is the wax itself and rubs off.

tips: When a passage adds "and in time it returns," that clause is usually the one the completion turns on.

whyCorrect: Clay from wet fields works its way to the bottom of the load, so a grab that always samples the top misses the soil that has settled. The sample then shows less soil than the load really carries, and the tare applied from it comes out too low. The error is worst exactly where the settling clay is — the wet-field loads.

whyWrong.B: Sampling above the settled clay produces too little soil in the sample, not too much, so the figures are understated rather than overstated.
whyWrong.C: Using the same grab all season keeps the method consistent but repeats the same bias every time; consistency is not accuracy.
whyWrong.D: The bias has a direction, because the clay always moves downward and the grab always samples upward.

whyCorrect: "A queen excluder is a grid whose gaps a worker can pass through and a queen cannot" is one complete clause, and "the brood stays below the grid and the honey is stored above it" is another. They are joined by the coordinating conjunction "so," which takes a comma before it when it links two independent clauses.

whyWrong.A: Without punctuation the two clauses run together as a fused sentence.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon already joins independent clauses on its own, so pairing it with "so" doubles the join.
whyWrong.C: A colon introduces an explanation or list directly and is not placed before a coordinating conjunction.

whyCorrect: "The rule that the chandlers of the old companies gave their apprentices was simple" is a complete independent clause, and what follows is the rule itself, spelled out. A colon is the mark that introduces an explanation or enumeration after a complete clause. The word "simple" makes a promise that the colon then delivers on.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and "never let the wick stand straight, and never let the wax boil" is a pair of imperatives functioning as the content of the rule, not a clause completing the thought.
whyWrong.B: With no mark at all, "was simple never let the wick stand straight" runs the announcement into the rule.
whyWrong.D: A comma is too weak to carry the break between a complete clause and the material it introduces, especially when that material already contains a comma.

whyCorrect: "that clear a patch of killed brood within two days" is essential to the sentence — it identifies which colonies are meant, and the word "only" makes that restriction explicit. A restrictive relative clause is never set off with commas, so the blank takes the bare "that."

whyWrong.B: A comma after "that" splits the relative pronoun from its own verb.
whyWrong.C: A comma before "that" would mark the clause as nonessential, but removing it leaves "The only colonies are the ones a breeder will take queens from," which no longer identifies anything.
whyWrong.D: This adds both faults at once, fencing an essential clause and cutting it off from its verb.

commonMistakes: Treating any long modifier as an interrupter. Ask first whether removing it destroys the sentence's meaning.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The number," which is singular; "of frames of comb a colony draws in a season" is a modifying phrase and cannot supply the subject. A singular subject takes "depends," and the present tense matches "it is given" later in the sentence.

whyWrong.A: "have depended" is plural and shifts to the present perfect for what is stated as a general truth.
whyWrong.B: "are depending" is plural, and the progressive misreports a standing fact as something in progress.
whyWrong.D: "depend" agrees with "frames," a noun inside the modifying phrase rather than the head of the subject.

tips: "The number of" is always singular; "a number of" is plural.

whyCorrect: "By the time the blockade was lifted in 1814" fixes a point in the past, and the building happened before it. An action completed before another past event takes the past perfect, so "had built" is required. The phrase "By the time …" is a reliable signal for this tense.

whyWrong.A: "builds" is present tense and cannot describe something finished by 1814.
whyWrong.B: "will build" places the construction in the future of the speaker, which contradicts the past framing.
whyWrong.D: "has built" links the action to the present moment, but the factories are said to have closed within five years of the peace.

whyCorrect: The readings belong to two thermometers, so a plural possessive is needed. A plural noun already ending in s forms its possessive with an apostrophe alone: thermometers'. "The two" before the blank fixes the number.

whyWrong.A: "thermometers's" adds a second s to a plural that already ends in one, which Standard English does not do.
whyWrong.C: "thermometer's" is the singular possessive and contradicts "The two."
whyWrong.D: With no apostrophe the word is a plain plural, leaving "readings" without the possessor the sentence needs.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the advantage of lifting late — maximum sugar — and the second gives the drawback that comes with the very same timing, the wettest fields and the highest tare. The transition has to hold a benefit and a cost together as two sides of one choice, which is what "At the same time" does.

whyWrong.A: A restatement would repeat the first sentence's point, but the second introduces a cost the first never mentioned.
whyWrong.C: The high tare is not caused by the roots holding more sugar; both simply follow from lifting late.
whyWrong.D: The second sentence is not an instance of roots holding the most sugar.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says the two sugars cannot be told apart, and the second says an instrument tells them apart easily. That is a direct opposition, so the transition must signal contrast.

whyWrong.B: "Likewise" claims the second sentence repeats the pattern of the first, but the two state opposite outcomes.
whyWrong.C: "Therefore" would make the spectrometer's success follow from the sugars being indistinguishable, which reverses the logic.
whyWrong.D: "In addition" adds a similar point, and the second sentence overturns the first rather than adding to it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes a conversion that works; the second withdraws it for the case that actually matters, since beet juice always holds more than sugar in solution. Introducing a limitation on the claim just made calls for a contrast transition.

whyWrong.A: "Similarly" would present the second sentence as another instance of the same thing working, which is the opposite of a limitation.
whyWrong.B: "Consequently" would make the restriction a consequence of the scale working, but the restriction is imposed from outside by what else is dissolved.
whyWrong.C: "Finally" marks the last item in a sequence, and no sequence of steps is being listed.

whyCorrect: The goal names two jobs, so the answer has to carry both: the impression identifies whose matrix made it, and the wax across the fold shows whether the letter has been opened. Only this choice puts the unreproducible impression and the broken fold together and names each function. A choice giving one job answers half the question.

whyWrong.A: This covers tamper evidence only, leaving identification out.
whyWrong.C: The reversed design in metal is background about the matrix, not a job the seal does.
whyWrong.D: Taking and holding the impression describes how the wax works, not the two purposes it served.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why some comb needs protecting and some does not, so the answer must give the distinction and its cause. This choice supplies the cause — the larvae eat cocoons and pollen, not clean wax — then both sides: comb that never held brood is safe, brood comb must be frozen or aired. A single note cannot draw a contrast.

whyWrong.B: This states the damage without saying which comb is at risk.
whyWrong.C: Freezing is one remedy, but nothing here explains why only some comb needs it.
whyWrong.D: This describes the treatment and omits the reason some comb can skip it.

whyCorrect: To show caramel is not merely melted sugar you need the chemistry — molecules broken into fragments that recombine into hundreds of new compounds — and evidence that the result is a different substance, which the loss of sweetness supplies. Only this choice carries the whole chain from breakdown to a colouring with no sweetness left.

whyWrong.A: This denies that caramel is melted sugar but stops before saying what it becomes instead.
whyWrong.B: The properties of the new compounds are given with no account of where they came from.
whyWrong.C: This is one consequence, and on its own it does not explain why the sweetness disappears.

whyCorrect: "glucose and fructose in quantity, with a trace of maltose" is a parenthetical list dropped into the middle of the sentence, and the dash before "glucose" opens it. A mark that opens a fence in mid-sentence has to close it with the matching mark, so a second dash is needed after "maltose." The clause that follows, "and the sucrose the bees began with survives in the smallest amounts of all," is the sentence continuing past the interruption, not another item in the list.

whyWrong.A: With nothing after "maltose" the dash is never closed, so the list runs on into the next clause and the reader cannot tell where the parenthetical ends.
whyWrong.C: A comma cannot close a fence that a dash opened; the two marks have to match.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon would have to join two independent clauses, but "glucose and fructose in quantity, with a trace of maltose" is a list of noun phrases with no verb.

tips: Dashes, like commas, work in pairs around an interruption — check that the mark closing the phrase matches the one that opened it.

whyCorrect: The passage sets "nothing sudden" against what the blank must name, and the evidence is that one passage marked nothing while tens of thousands of passages cut grooves deep enough to take a hand. The force was small but never stopped. Relentless is the word for something that acts continuously over a long time rather than violently in a moment.

whyWrong.A: Violent is what the sentence rules out with "nothing sudden"; the point is that no single pass did any damage.
whyWrong.B: The grooves took tens of thousands of passages, so the process was long rather than recent.
whyWrong.C: Nobody intended to cut the stone; the wear is a by-product of towing.

whyCorrect: Every detail in the passage is about movement: huts at the end of the cutting, leaving when the work was done, gangs going off to another line for a penny more a day. That is a workforce with no fixed place of work. Itinerant names exactly that, and it pairs with "skilled" as the second half of what made them hard to keep.

whyWrong.B: The men left for a penny more a day, which shows they had bargaining power; poverty is never described.
whyWrong.C: No ages are given anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.D: Organised bargaining is not mentioned; the men moved as individual gangs chasing a better rate.

commonMistakes: Choosing a word that fits a general picture of nineteenth-century labourers instead of the one trait the passage actually documents.

whyCorrect: The text spells out the cost of not knowing: a boatman who runs past a winding hole has to work on for miles before he can turn. That makes the knowledge practical and necessary rather than decorative. The blank is contrasted with "a nicety of the trade," so it has to mean essential.

whyWrong.A: Theoretical would mean knowledge with no practical use, which contradicts the whole passage.
whyWrong.C: Ornamental is a near-synonym of the "nicety" the sentence sets the blank against.
whyWrong.D: Nothing suggests the bays had gone out of use; they are described as in service.

whyCorrect: The arm is described as cut from the main line, wide enough for two boats to pass, ending at a wall, with traffic leaving the main line at a junction and returning to it. Everything about it is a waterway. The word here means a subsidiary channel running off a larger one.

whyWrong.A: A division of an organisation would be a group of people, but this arm is dug and has boats in it.
whyWrong.B: The literal body sense does not fit something cut through ground and filled with water.
whyWrong.D: The weapon sense is unrelated to anything in the passage.

tips: For a familiar word with several senses, let the surrounding nouns decide — here they are all physical features of a canal.

whyCorrect: The method described is four hours of pushing a boat along a tunnel wall with your feet, in the cold and the dark, and crews paid a tug fee to escape it as soon as they could afford to. The blank has to name the quality that made them willing to pay. Laborious captures the sheer physical effort the passage documents.

whyWrong.B: Legging is ingenious in its way, but ingenuity would be no reason to abandon it the moment money allowed.
whyWrong.C: Customary explains that it was usual, not why crews gave it up.
whyWrong.D: Legging cost nothing and the tug cost a fee, so if anything it was the cheaper option — which is why the passage stresses raising the fee.

whyCorrect: The text opens by saying two jobs look alike and are not, separates them by what they remove and how often each is needed, and closes with committees that combined them in the accounts and could not explain their own figures. The purpose is to show that the difference has financial consequences. The last sentence tells you what is at stake.

whyWrong.A: Frequencies are given to distinguish the two jobs, not to recommend doing either one more often.
whyWrong.B: No machinery is described at all.
whyWrong.C: Rates of silting in different lengths never come up; the comparison is between two operations.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence supplies the mechanism — a boat displaces exactly its own weight of water, which runs out of the trough — and the last draws the conclusion that one boat, none or a queue all leave the piers carrying the same load. The text exists to explain that result. Look for the fact the closing sentence is built on.

whyWrong.A: No engineer is named and no career is recounted.
whyWrong.C: Construction methods are not described; the text is about loads, not building.
whyWrong.D: Masonry aqueducts are never mentioned, so no comparison is argued.

whyCorrect: Text 1 attributes the collapse to speed. Text 2 opens by saying speed mattered less than that supposes, then gives the real constraint: a canal company's charges were capped by its Act, so it could not cross-subsidise a rate cut, while railway companies were bound far more loosely. That is a difference in commercial freedom being mistaken for a difference in technology.

whyWrong.A: Text 2 assumes railways did cut rates — that freedom is the centre of its argument.
whyWrong.C: Text 2 does not concede that speed was decisive; it argues the opposite.
whyWrong.D: Text 2 says the bulk of canal tonnage was coal, stone and timber and "none of it was urgent."

whyCorrect: The pivot is the second sentence: companies could not prevent every breach, so they set out to limit what one would cost. The stop gates then do exactly that, sealing automatically and confining the loss to the length between one pair and the next. A main idea has to include both the abandoned aim and the substituted one.

whyWrong.A: The gates are described as tripped by the rush of water itself, not closed by a keeper responding to a report.
whyWrong.B: The text says the loss stops at the length between one pair of gates and the next, which is the opposite of the whole canal emptying.
whyWrong.D: Nothing is abandoned; the embanked lengths are protected and kept in use.

whyCorrect: The problem stated first is rain stopping work across an open quay. The solution runs the channel in under the building so goods rise through trapdoors, and the closing sentence names both gains: nothing waited on the weather and no cart was needed. The main idea must carry both.

whyWrong.B: Quay size is never mentioned; it was the rain that stopped the work.
whyWrong.C: No costs of any kind are given.
whyWrong.D: Damp on the upper floors is not discussed; the hoists are about moving goods, not preserving them.

whyCorrect: To choose between wear and deliberate cutting, look for evidence that ties the grooves to where a rope actually rubbed. Grooves absent where the rope never crossed the corner, and deepest where it crossed at the sharpest angle, match the pattern of friction and not the pattern of a builder's decision. The strongest support is a correlation the rival explanation cannot produce.

whyWrong.B: Grooves on bridges no boat passed under would count against the tow-rope explanation, not for it.
whyWrong.C: Surviving timber posts support the rubbing-post explanation instead.
whyWrong.D: Softer stone would explain why grooves formed easily under either explanation, so it does not separate the two.

whyCorrect: The society's reply is that the plants will persist in margins and lightly used pounds even after restoration. A line reopened twenty years ago still holding those plants at pre-restoration densities in exactly those places is a direct test of that prediction. It supplies the after-restoration evidence the claim needs.

whyWrong.A: Rising traffic makes the society's case harder, not easier.
whyWrong.B: This supports the ecologists by showing how rich the derelict length is.
whyWrong.D: Plants growing elsewhere in the county says nothing about whether they survive in a restored canal, which is what the reply asserted.

whyCorrect: Aldwinckle's claim has two parts: the written order mattered less, and the deference of other crews mattered more. This quotation gives both — a crew drawing aside "without a word said, as any crew would," and the order never once produced. A quotation showing only that the order existed misses the point of the claim.

whyWrong.A: Changing horses and not tying up describe how fly boats were run, not how other crews treated them.
whyWrong.C: This documents the written order, which is the thing Aldwinckle says was not what did the work.
whyWrong.D: A night in a tunnel is incidental detail with no bearing on precedence at a lock.

whyCorrect: The only difference the text gives between the two linings is what happens when they dry out: puddle cracks and will not reseal, concrete does not care. So the change matters most where drying out is likely — a canal emptied for long repairs or left without water for years. Match the completion to the single property the passage contrasted.

whyWrong.A: Wealth and masons are never mentioned, and the difference described is about water, not workmanship.
whyWrong.C: Cargo weight and speed have nothing to do with a lining drying out.
whyWrong.D: An embankment raises the consequences of a breach, which the passage does not connect to the puddle-versus-concrete difference.

whyCorrect: The cost the passage describes is a labour cost: at an ordinary bridge someone has to stop, cast off, lead the horse over and pick the line up while the boat is still moving. That is two jobs at once, and the turnover bridge removes the need to do them because the line never comes off. The design is therefore worth most to a boat with only one pair of hands aboard.

whyWrong.A: Changing horses is a separate operation the text never links to towpath changes, and a large crew is the case where the difficulty least applies.
whyWrong.B: Ownership of the bridges has no bearing on the handling problem the passage sets out.
whyWrong.C: Perishable cargo would make speed matter, but the text describes an awkwardness of handling rather than a delay.

whyCorrect: "Floated empty in a gauging dock and then loaded a ton at a time with iron weights" is a participial phrase opening the sentence, and "each new boat yielded a table" is the main clause. An introductory participial phrase is separated from the clause it modifies by a comma. The phrase has no subject or finite verb of its own, which is what tells you it is not a clause.

whyWrong.A: A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and a participial phrase is not one.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation the phrase runs into the subject and "weights each new boat" reads as a single unit.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and the opening phrase is not independent.

whyCorrect: "Weed cutting removes what has grown in the water this season" and "dredging takes out what has settled on the bed over many" are both complete clauses with no conjunction between them. A semicolon is the mark for joining two independent clauses, and it also points up the parallel between them.

whyWrong.A: With nothing between them the two clauses are fused, and "this season dredging" reads as one phrase.
whyWrong.B: A colon introduces something the first clause has promised to explain or list; here the second clause contrasts with the first rather than unpacking it.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two independent clauses without a conjunction is a comma splice.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The man who walked a fixed beat of bank every day," and everything from "watching" to "lengthsman" is a nonrestrictive modifier opened by the comma after "day." That modifier has to be closed with a matching comma before the main verb "was paid." Look for the mark that opened the interruption and give it its partner.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and what precedes it is a subject with its modifiers but no verb.
whyWrong.B: A colon must follow a complete independent clause, which this is not until "was paid" arrives.
whyWrong.D: With no mark the modifier is left open at the end while the comma after "day" still opens it, so the fencing is unmatched.

whyCorrect: The sentence is inverted: the opening phrase "Hanging on a hook inside the cabin door of every working boat" is a modifier, and the real subject follows the verb — "the windlasses," which is plural. A verb agrees with its subject whatever the word order, so the plural "are" is required. Turn the sentence round to check: "The windlasses … are hanging on a hook."

whyWrong.A: "was" is singular and agrees with nothing in the sentence; "boat" and "door" sit inside prepositional phrases and cannot be the subject.
whyWrong.B: "has been" is also singular, and the perfect adds a completed-action sense the sentence does not want.
whyWrong.D: "is" is singular, again matching "boat" rather than the plural subject "windlasses."

commonMistakes: Letting the nearest noun before the verb decide agreement. In an inverted sentence the subject comes after the verb.

whyCorrect: The auxiliary "had" requires a past participle, and the past participle of freeze is "frozen." The sentence needs the past perfect because the freezing came before the three weeks of stoppage being described.

whyWrong.A: "froze" is the simple past, which cannot follow "had."
whyWrong.B: "freezed" is not a form of the verb; freeze is irregular.
whyWrong.C: "freezing" is the present participle, which after "had" would need "been" in front of it and would still give the wrong meaning.

whyCorrect: "Cut through gravel and lined with clay trodden until it was uniform" is a participial phrase, and the noun right after the comma must be the thing that was cut and lined. That is the channel. Any other subject leaves the phrase modifying something that was never dug.

whyWrong.A: This makes "engineers" the thing cut through gravel and lined with clay.
whyWrong.B: The subject becomes "keeping the lining wet," a gerund phrase that cannot have been cut or lined.
whyWrong.C: The empty "it" of "it was necessary" gives the participle nothing to attach to.

tips: Read only as far as the first noun after the comma — that noun has to be what the opening phrase describes.

whyCorrect: The first sentence sets out a problem in two halves: goods exposed overnight, and constables whose authority stopped at the parish boundary. The second gives the companies' answer — their own constables with power along the whole navigation. That is a response caused by the problem, so a result transition is needed.

whyWrong.A: The company constables are not an example of the problem; they are the remedy for it.
whyWrong.B: "By contrast" implies the two sentences oppose each other, but the second solves what the first describes.
whyWrong.C: "In addition" would make the Acts another item in a list of difficulties rather than the answer to them.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says legging was slow and badly paid, which would lead you to expect crews to give it up as soon as a tug existed. The second says they carried on for twenty years anyway. The transition has to mark that the expected result did not follow, which is a concession.

whyWrong.B: "As a result" would make continuing to leg a consequence of its being unpleasant, which is backwards.
whyWrong.C: "In other words" signals a restatement, but the second sentence introduces new and opposing information.
whyWrong.D: The persistence of these crews is not an example of legging being slow and badly paid.

whyCorrect: The goal is the circumstances in which a horse-marine was taken, so the answer must give the condition and the response together: the carrier's own horses covered fixed stages, and traffic beyond them was worked with a hired horse and driver. This choice states the limit and what filled it. The other options list facts without linking a situation to the practice.

whyWrong.A: This pairs two facts but never says that hiring happened when traffic ran beyond the stages, so no circumstance is identified.
whyWrong.C: This defines the term and its source without saying when a carrier would resort to it.
whyWrong.D: Stabling arrangements alone give no occasion for hiring anything.

whyCorrect: To say what the Act was meant to control, the answer needs the condition it addressed — families living in cabins eight feet by seven — and the mechanism it created, a registered limit on how many might sleep aboard and an inspector able to count them. Only this choice puts the crowding and the enforceable limit together. The others give the Act without its target or the target without the Act.

whyWrong.A: This describes the overcrowding but never mentions the Act, so nothing is being controlled.
whyWrong.B: Registration alone does not say what registration was for.
whyWrong.C: This gives the machinery of enforcement without the crowding that made it necessary.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain why one lock could govern a whole route, which needs the asymmetry — a wide barge cannot get through a narrow lock, though a narrow boat passes either — and the consequence, that a route admits only craft small enough for its tightest point. This choice supplies the cause and the rule together.

whyWrong.B: Two regional lock widths are the background; on their own they explain nothing about a route.
whyWrong.C: This states the harmless direction of the asymmetry and leaves out the direction that causes the problem.
whyWrong.D: This asserts the rule but gives no reason for it, adding only a fact about the northern locks.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states the general practice: bridges were numbered and boatmen used the numbers instead of place names. The second sentence puts a specific case to it — a boat lying below bridge ninety-four — to show what that practice looked like in use. Moving from a general habit to one concrete instance of it calls for an exemplifying transition, and the particular number is the giveaway.

whyWrong.A: "Even so" concedes something that cuts against the previous sentence, but the example confirms it.
whyWrong.C: "By contrast" would set the two sentences in opposition, and they agree completely.
whyWrong.D: "Consequently" would present bridge ninety-four as an effect of the numbering rather than as an illustration of boatmen using it; the sentence supplies a specimen, not a result.

whyCorrect: The V pointing upstream means the water pressure, which would burst a flat gate, instead pushes the leaves harder together and harder onto the stone. The threatening force is doing the sealing. Enlists is the word for turning something hostile into an agent of your own purpose.

whyWrong.A: Nothing is hidden; the pressure is fully present and doing work.
whyWrong.C: Withstanding is what a flat gate would try to do, and the passage's point is that this design does something cleverer than merely resisting.
whyWrong.D: No measurement is taken anywhere in the text.

tips: When a sentence says a design uses "the very force that threatens it," the word must express co-opting, not resisting.

whyCorrect: The engine cost money every day but paid off only in a dry summer nobody could foresee. That is the structure of a premium paid against an uncertain loss. Insurance is the word for a steady cost accepted to protect against an occasional and unpredictable one.

whyWrong.A: Capacity would mean more traffic could be carried, but the engine recycles water rather than enlarging the line.
whyWrong.B: Goodwill concerns reputation, and the directors are described as buying protection against weather.
whyWrong.D: Prestige is not mentioned, and a pumping engine at the foot of a lock flight is a working expense, not a display.

whyCorrect: With a private channel to a basin under its own walls, a mill no longer needed the cart, the public wharf or the quarter-mile haul at all. The blank names what the digging bought, and it bought the removal of that step. Elimination is the word for doing away with something completely.

whyWrong.A: Regulation would mean the cartage continued under rules, but it stopped.
whyWrong.B: Postponement implies the cartage still had to happen later, which is not what a basin under the mill achieves.
whyWrong.C: A subsidy would mean someone else paid for the cartage; the mill paid for the digging instead and had no cartage left.

whyCorrect: Every feature listed serves speed: two crews sleeping in turn so the boat never stops, fresh horses at stages, and priority at locks. The sentence sets this against "the leisurely progress of the coal traffic," so the blank must be the opposite of leisurely. Expeditious means done quickly and efficiently.

whyWrong.A: Nothing ties the service to a time of year; it ran continuously.
whyWrong.B: The fly boat carried a company order granting it precedence, so it was governed by rules rather than free of them.
whyWrong.D: The passage says the traffic "paid for the privilege," which makes the service dear rather than cheap.

whyCorrect: The colon introduces the reason: rock too slowly and the ice closes again behind the boat. That makes the rate of rocking the thing that had to be got right, and the men are described as rocking "in time." Timed names the control the failure case points to.

whyWrong.A: Concealment has nothing to do with an ice boat working in the open with a dozen men aboard.
whyWrong.B: No record is kept; the passage is about how the boat was worked, not what was written down.
whyWrong.C: Cost never appears, and pricing an action cannot stop ice closing behind a hull.

tips: When a colon follows the blank, read what comes after it — the explanation usually names the missing word.

whyCorrect: Before the underlined sentence the text is entirely historical: towpaths were company property and walkers were tolerated trespassers. After it the text is entirely modern: access by agreement rather than right, and closure without highway procedure. The sentence names the link between the two — "That history explains the odd position the paths occupy now."

whyWrong.B: Nothing in the text disputes it; the sentences after it supply the evidence for it.
whyWrong.C: No individual towpath is named or described as closed.
whyWrong.D: No legal term is defined; the sentences that follow describe arrangements rather than explain a word.
