whyCorrect: The text sets out the old arrangement — gangs of men hauling from an unmade bank — then the change to a fenced, made path, then the consequence, that a horse on a firm path could outdo six men and the bow hauliers disappeared wherever such a path existed. The final clause clinches the causal link by noting they survived only where the bank was unimproved. The purpose is to explain that displacement.

whyWrong.B: The hauliers' fate is described without any judgement about fairness.
whyWrong.C: The path is called made, fenced and let to toll-payers, but nothing about how it was built is described.
whyWrong.D: Steam towage never appears, and no costs are given.

whyCorrect: Text 1 calls the tug a straightforward improvement nobody would have refused. Text 2 accepts the time saving but points out that the charge fell on the carrier regardless of what the cargo could bear, so the fly boat could sell its three hours and the coal boat could not. That is a claim about who the saving was worth paying for, not about whether the saving existed.

whyWrong.A: Text 2 accepts the forty minutes against four hours and builds its argument on the three hours saved.
whyWrong.B: Text 2 never questions the strain; it argues about cost.
whyWrong.C: Text 2 says the opposite — crews went on legging until the company forbade it two decades later.

whyCorrect: The mud went over the gunwale onto the field side, the side away from the towpath, and a century of it raised that side into a low ridge with the water sitting visibly above the meadow beyond. That is the stated consequence. The question asks for a result of the disposal method, so trace what the tipping produced.

whyWrong.A: The hawthorn seeded itself, which the text says explicitly; nobody planted it.
whyWrong.C: Dredging removes material from the channel, and the text describes no loss of depth.
whyWrong.D: The passage says the cheapest disposal was over the side, and no obligation to carry it away is mentioned.

whyCorrect: The last sentence states the effect directly: the through rate came out higher than the sum of what either company would have charged on its own. The compensation toll added a payment on top of the two companies' ordinary charges, so crossing a junction cost more than the two charges combined.

whyWrong.A: The extra payment passed between the companies; the text does not describe the same company charging a boat twice.
whyWrong.C: The text says the arrangement kept the junctions open.
whyWrong.D: The direction is reversed — the second, newer company paid the first for traffic it had taken.

whyCorrect: The argument is that on some pounds restricting traffic saves less than repairing the lining, so you need a pound where leakage exceeds lockage. Ryebank lost 5,600 cubic metres through bed and banks against 2,940 through the locks — the leak is close to twice everything the traffic took. Stopping all 21 boats would not save what the lining is losing.

whyWrong.A: The summit is the opposite case: 8,680 through the locks against 1,150 through bed and banks, which argues for restricting traffic there.
whyWrong.B: Comparing boat numbers at Marsh and the summit says nothing about which kind of loss dominates.
whyWrong.C: A total for Highfield ignores the split between the two kinds of loss, which is the whole basis of the argument.

commonMistakes: Citing a true figure from the table that does not bear on the specific claim — here the claim is about the ratio of the two losses, not about totals.

whyCorrect: To show speed matters more than volume of traffic, you need a pair where the busier site loses less bank. Ashlock had a limit, carried 3,100 boats a year and lost 4 cm; Denbrook had no limit, carried 1,450 and lost 11 cm. More than twice the traffic and about a third of the retreat is exactly the pattern the conclusion needs.

whyWrong.B: Bramble's 19 cm is the largest retreat, but citing one site alone shows nothing about which factor caused it.
whyWrong.C: This compares traffic levels only and never mentions bank retreat or the limits.
whyWrong.D: Coldwell's 3 cm is the least, yet Coldwell also has the lightest traffic, so on its own it cannot separate speed from volume.

tips: To argue that one variable outweighs another, cite a case where the two point in opposite directions.

whyCorrect: The company's explanation is that the engine held the summit up. The way to weaken it is a period when the engine was working but the other suspected causes were not. Two dry summers after the engine and before the reservoir was enlarged, with the summit falling to its old levels, show the engine alone achieving nothing.

whyWrong.A: What other companies did says nothing about whether this engine worked.
whyWrong.C: Burning more coal in dry years shows the engine ran harder when needed, which fits the company's account rather than undermining it.
whyWrong.D: Rising traffic removes one of the historian's alternatives and so strengthens the company's case.

whyCorrect: The passage gives one reason water carriage loses its advantage: hardly anything now stands on the water, so goods are lifted twice and hauled by road at each end. Remove that condition and the advantage survives, which means both ends of the journey have to be on the waterway itself. The completion must undo precisely the disadvantage the text named.

whyWrong.B: The cost described is the double handling and the road legs, not the type of lifting gear.
whyWrong.C: Journey length is never mentioned; the barge's fuel advantage grows with distance if anything.
whyWrong.D: Fuel is where the barge already wins, so a change in fuel prices does not address the road haulage that cancels the win.

whyCorrect: The passage contrasts two positions: a wage boatman keeps drawing pay through a freeze, while an owner's earnings stop completely and his costs — horse and family — carry on. Whoever bears the whole loss of a stoppage has the strongest interest in preventing one. So the owner is the one who would pay towards keeping a channel open in frost.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the text ties his earnings to delivery within a day; the problem is a stoppage lasting as long as the frost.
whyWrong.B: Tolls are never mentioned, and the threat the passage identifies is ice.
whyWrong.D: More locks mean slower passage and more water used, which does nothing for a man paid by delivery.

whyCorrect: "Ice forming in the joints of a lock wall lifts every stone a fraction each winter" and "the coping has to be taken up and reset long before the stone itself is anywhere near worn away" are both independent clauses. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma goes before it.

whyWrong.B: Without the comma two full clauses are joined by a bare conjunction.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon replaces the conjunction rather than accompanying it, so "; and" doubles the join.
whyWrong.D: A colon introduces an explanation or list directly and is not used before a coordinating conjunction.

whyCorrect: "in the dry August of 1826 the summit was down to eighteen inches over the sill and all traffic stopped for a fortnight" is a complete sentence, and so is everything before the blank. Two independent clauses with no conjunction need a full stop between them here, because the second contrasts the dry year with the wet one rather than explaining it.

whyWrong.A: A colon promises that what follows will explain or specify the first clause, but the second clause switches to the opposite case.
whyWrong.C: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation "very little of what they hold in the dry August of 1826" reads as one phrase and the second clause loses its subject.

whyCorrect: "Because the top gate of one chamber is at the same time the bottom gate of the next" is a subordinate clause opening the sentence, and "two boats cannot pass one another anywhere on a staircase" is the main clause. A dependent clause placed first is separated from the main clause by a comma.

whyWrong.B: With no comma, "the next two" reads as a single phrase and the boundary between the clauses vanishes.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and a "Because" clause is dependent.
whyWrong.D: A colon must be preceded by an independent clause, which this is not.

whyCorrect: The ledgers belong to the wharfinger, so the relative pronoun has to be possessive: "the wharfinger whose ledgers survive at Norbrook." Whose is the possessive relative pronoun and is the only option that can stand in front of the noun "ledgers."

whyWrong.B: "who's" is the contraction of who is, giving "the wharfinger who is ledgers survive."
whyWrong.C: "who" is a subject pronoun and would need its own verb; here it is followed immediately by a noun.
whyWrong.D: "which" refers to things rather than people, and it is also not possessive.

whyCorrect: The subject is "Two," which is plural; "of the tunnels on the northern section" is a prepositional phrase and cannot supply the subject. The second half of the sentence uses "had to be worked," so the tense is past, and the plural past form is "were."

whyWrong.A: "has been" is singular and shifts to the present perfect.
whyWrong.B: "is" is singular and present, clashing with both the plural subject and the past narration.
whyWrong.D: "was" has the right tense but is singular, agreeing with "section" rather than with "Two."

whyCorrect: "Had the committee carried the line over the ridge …" is an inverted past counterfactual — it means "If the committee had carried." The main clause of a past counterfactual takes would have plus a past participle, so "would have been finished" is required. The matching "no crew would ever have had to leg a boat" later in the sentence confirms the pattern.

whyWrong.A: "will have been finished" is a future perfect and treats the works as still to come.
whyWrong.B: "had been finished" repeats the if-clause tense in the result clause, which leaves the sentence with two conditions and no consequence.
whyWrong.D: "would be finished" is the present counterfactual and clashes with a condition set firmly in the past.

whyCorrect: Both sentences describe the same kind of convenience: a document that let a clerk settle something without inspecting anything. The gauging table replaced opening the holds; the classification schedule replaced examining the goods. Two parallel instances call for a transition of likeness.

whyWrong.A: The schedule is not caused by the gauging table; they are separate devices doing similar work.
whyWrong.B: "In fact" intensifies or corrects the previous statement, and the second sentence does neither.
whyWrong.D: "However" would set the two in opposition, but they make the same point.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives one advantage of the tug — the time saved — and the second adds a different one, the end of work that ruined men's backs. Adding a further point of the same kind calls for an additive transition.

whyWrong.A: "In short" introduces a summary, and the second sentence brings in something the first never mentioned.
whyWrong.B: "Otherwise" states what would happen in the absence of the first sentence's condition, which is not the relationship here.
whyWrong.D: "Instead" would replace the first sentence's claim, but both remain true.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives a freedom: rates could be cut without limit. The second takes away the matching freedom in the other direction, since the ceiling was already reached. A transition marking that limitation has to be contrastive.

whyWrong.A: "Therefore" would make the inability to raise rates a consequence of being free to cut them, but the two come from different parts of the Act.
whyWrong.B: The second sentence is a separate restriction, not an instance of the freedom just described.
whyWrong.C: "Similarly" claims the two sentences make the same point, and they are opposites.

whyCorrect: The audience already knows how gauging works, so the answer should be the clerk's own procedure rather than a rehearsal of how the tables were made. This choice gives exactly that — measure the freeboard, read the weight off the table for that hull — with just enough of the table's origin to identify it. The other options describe the preparation and never reach the clerk.

whyWrong.B: This is the calibration of the boat, which the audience is assumed to know already, and it never mentions the clerk.
whyWrong.C: Where the tables were kept is logistics, not the method of arriving at a weight.
whyWrong.D: This combines two preparatory steps and stops before the toll house reading.

whyCorrect: For readers who already know iron aqueducts, the point to explain is the bedding: flannel dipped in white lead at the flanged joints, which allows slight movement while staying watertight. This choice names the material and states what it achieves. The others describe expansion or bolting, which the informed audience already assumes.

whyWrong.A: Bolted flanged joints are the ordinary construction and say nothing about accommodating movement.
whyWrong.B: This pairs expansion with the bedding but never says the bedding permits movement without leaking, which is the thing to be explained.
whyWrong.D: Both halves are background the audience is assumed to know, and neither mentions the flannel bedding.

whyCorrect: To emphasise the limits of the evidence you have to name the gap and say what it prevents. No boat painted before 1858 carries the pattern, so neither rival account can be checked against an earlier example — the record simply stops before the question begins. A choice that merely reports one side's theory does not address the evidence at all.

whyWrong.A: This states one hypothesis without indicating how well it can be tested.
whyWrong.B: This states the rival hypothesis and adds a claim about house styles that the notes never make.
whyWrong.D: This describes the pattern and its date range, presenting the evidence rather than pointing out what it cannot settle.

whyCorrect: The first sentence defines the word for you: the water between one lock and the next lies dead level, and "it is this level stretch, not the lock, that a boatman calls a pound." Everything after that treats a pound as a body of water with a length and a depth that can be drawn down. The technical sense is the stretch of water itself.

whyWrong.B: The hammering sense is a verb here and cannot be something that holds water.
whyWrong.C: A unit of weight cannot be long or short, or refilled from above.
whyWrong.D: The animal-enclosure sense is a real meaning of the word but nothing in this passage involves animals.

tips: When a passage says "what a boatman calls a X," the definition is usually in that same sentence.

whyCorrect: The two short sentences before the blank do the work: "The bank is the company's to repair; the day saved belongs to the carrier." The cost falls on one party and the benefit on another, so the two are separate parties with opposed interests — which is why a limit had to be imposed rather than left to agreement.

whyWrong.A: Cooperative would mean the two worked together, which is the opposite of a situation needing a rule imposed on one of them.
whyWrong.B: The company knew perfectly well whose boats were passing; identity is not the issue.
whyWrong.D: Negligent would blame the carrier for carelessness, but the passage describes him rationally pursuing a saving that costs him nothing.

whyCorrect: Each reach is named as a piece of the waterway itself — the two miles below the junction, the straight above the aqueduct, the curve at the mill — and silt is lifted from each. The word is being used for a continuous length of navigation. The list after the colon is the definition in disguise.

whyWrong.A: A distance that can be covered would be a measurement, not something with a curve at a mill.
whyWrong.C: The audience sense of the word has no bearing on a survey of silt.
whyWrong.D: The physical act of stretching an arm cannot be divided into miles and priced for maintenance.

whyCorrect: Money went into lines whose route had not been surveyed, on nothing more than a river's name and a promise of coal, and a third of the authorised companies had cut no channel six years later. That is capital committed on hope rather than on information. Speculative is the word for investment made on an unexamined prospect.

whyWrong.A: Collaborative describes how investors worked together, which the passage does not discuss.
whyWrong.C: Lists filling within hours indicates a rush of money, not restraint.
whyWrong.D: The Acts authorised the companies but the passage shows nothing checking what investors bought into.

whyCorrect: The schedule set different maxima for different classes — a few pence a ton for coal and limestone, several times as much for manufactures over the same water. A scale that rises by class is a graduated one, and that is exactly why the clerk's classification mattered so much to a trader.

whyWrong.B: Uniform means the same throughout, which the sentence before the blank explicitly denies.
whyWrong.C: Provisional would mean temporary, but the schedule was fixed by the company's Act.
whyWrong.D: Confidential is ruled out by traders knowing the rates well enough to care which class applied.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence states the crucial property of puddle: it has no strength of its own and must stay wet. The sentence after it draws the working consequence — a lining cracked beyond saving if drained in summer, so heavy work is done in winter and the length refilled as soon as the masons are clear. The sentence supplies the reason those practices exist.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the text rejects the claim; the rest of the passage builds on it.
whyWrong.B: Puddle was already defined in the previous sentence as clay worked and trodden; this sentence adds a property instead.
whyWrong.C: Only one lining material is discussed.

whyCorrect: The sentence explains why the fraud was undetectable from inside the company: the ledger recorded only the declaration, so a false declaration produced a clean-looking record. The next sentence begins "Check clerks were therefore stationed along the line," which makes the underlined sentence the reason an outside check was necessary. Look at the "therefore" that follows it.

whyWrong.A: No second fraud appears; the sentence is about the same false declaration already described.
whyWrong.B: It states one link in the argument rather than summarising the whole of it, and the text continues past it.
whyWrong.D: Nothing suggests the sums were trivial; the company went to the expense of stationing check clerks.

whyCorrect: Text 2 does not object to restoration itself; it objects to calling the result a recovery when, measured by what lives there, it is an "exchange." The scarce shallow weedy habitat goes and the dredged navigable channel arrives, so one community of species replaces another. That is a substitution, not a plain gain.

whyWrong.A: Text 2 says explicitly that ecologists do not object to restoration as such, and it makes no engineering criticism.
whyWrong.B: This reverses the position: Text 2 is the one withholding the word improvement.
whyWrong.D: Text 2's whole argument is that what lives in the channel changes.

whyCorrect: The passage gives the reason plainly: "The animal ate whether it worked or not." A carrier with a light trade would be feeding a horse on many idle days, so the fixed cost of ownership outweighs the higher daily rate of hire. The closing clause confirms it by noting the hire rate would have ruined him only if he had needed the horse every day.

whyWrong.A: No comparison of strength is made anywhere.
whyWrong.B: Innkeepers are described as hiring out horses and stabling, not refusing service.
whyWrong.C: No company requirement is mentioned; the choice is the carrier's own.

whyCorrect: The text builds one chain: a staircase has no pounds, the top gate of one chamber is the bottom gate of the next, so a descending boat needs every chamber below it empty and an ascending one every chamber above it full. That makes the two requirements incompatible, and one boat must be worked right through before the other starts. The main idea is that shared gates force sequential working.

whyWrong.B: Total rise is never compared between the two arrangements.
whyWrong.C: Water use is not discussed, and a staircase in fact passes the whole volume down through every chamber.
whyWrong.D: No difference in speed between ascending and descending boats is stated.

whyCorrect: The emphasis to be illustrated is disorientation, not the leggers' labour. This quotation is entirely about losing one's bearings — no up nor down, and no way of telling whether the boat was moving except a drip on the cabin roof. It reports a state of perception rather than an event.

whyWrong.A: The men's hard breathing is precisely the labour the stem says Marbury does not dwell on.
whyWrong.B: A timed passage and a fern-hung cutting are observation and record, not disorientation.
whyWrong.C: The horse sent over the hill is a piece of practical arrangement.

whyCorrect: The conclusion is that a small share of tonnage can matter more to income than its weight suggests, so the citation has to pair a small tonnage with a large receipt. Manufactured goods are 16,000 tons of roughly 357,000 — under five per cent — yet return £2,700 against £2,400 from stone, sand and lime, which weigh six times as much. That is the mismatch the conclusion describes.

whyWrong.A: Timber earning less than coal shows the larger tonnage earning more, which is the ordinary pattern the conclusion is contrasted with.
whyWrong.B: This compares tonnages only and never brings in receipts.
whyWrong.D: Coal earning the most while also carrying the most is exactly what its size suggests.

commonMistakes: Quoting one column. A claim that weight and income come apart needs both columns for the same class.

whyCorrect: The claim is that the committee deferred rather than decided. This minute does exactly that: the engine goes back to the works committee "once more," with the mild season offered as the reason for not settling it. The words "referred once more" are the resistance in action.

whyWrong.A: Enlarging a reservoir is a decision taken, and it concerns a different work altogether.
whyWrong.B: A report on the lining between two locks has nothing to do with the pumping engine.
whyWrong.D: Ordering the engine erected without delay is the opposite of resisting the expense.

whyCorrect: The passage sets a capped canal company against loosely bound railways that could cut one rate and recover the loss on another. The cap is a maximum, so the canal company could always go down but never up. What it could not do, therefore, is recoup a cut by charging the remaining traffic more — its rates were already at the ceiling.

whyWrong.B: Nothing in the text describes goods falling outside the classes; the Act is said to state a maximum for each class.
whyWrong.C: Cutting below the maximum is exactly what the passage says the company could do.
whyWrong.D: Applying to Parliament is never mentioned as barred; the constraint described is the ceiling on rates.

whyCorrect: The passage says the pressure of the higher water is what holds the leaves shut, and that a gate cannot be pushed open until the paddles are drawn and the levels equalise. An immovable gate is therefore the normal behaviour of a gate with unequal water on its two sides, not a fault. The completion has to name that condition rather than a defect.

whyWrong.A: Damaged ironwork is a possible fault but the passage offers no reason to reach for it, and the sentence explicitly rules out the gate being jammed.
whyWrong.B: Boat width has nothing to do with whether a gate swings; the text never mentions the chamber's dimensions.
whyWrong.C: No locking of gates against unauthorised use appears anywhere in the passage.

tips: When a passage explains a mechanism, the inference has to be the mechanism working normally, not a breakdown of it.

whyCorrect: "plank grooves, in the company's language" is a parenthetical renaming of the slots, and the dash before it opens the interruption. A dash that opens a mid-sentence interruption has to be closed by a matching dash, after which the main verb "were" continues the sentence. Marks that fence a phrase must come in pairs of the same kind.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and everything before it is a subject with modifiers and no verb.
whyWrong.C: A comma cannot close a fence that a dash opened, and the appositive already contains a comma of its own.
whyWrong.D: With no mark, the appositive is never closed while the opening dash still stands, so the reader cannot tell where the interruption ends.

whyCorrect: Everything from "who walked" to "stayed at the tiller" is a restrictive relative clause identifying which boy is meant, and the main verb is "took." A restrictive clause takes no punctuation, and nothing may separate a subject from its verb, so the blank stays bare.

whyWrong.A: A comma here cuts the subject off from its own verb, and no comma opened the clause to be matched.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides; the subject and its relative clause form no clause without "took."
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and the sentence is not complete until the main verb arrives.

commonMistakes: Inserting a comma because the subject is long. Length is not a reason to punctuate — structure is.

whyCorrect: "The company's Act named three classes of goods and fixed a separate maximum rate for each" is a complete independent clause, and the three classes are then listed. A colon is the mark that introduces a list after a complete clause. The word "three" is the announcement the colon delivers on.

whyWrong.A: A comma is not the mark for introducing a list that follows a complete clause, and here it would read as if "coal" were in apposition to "each."
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation "for each coal" runs the pronoun into the first list item.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon joins independent clauses, and a list of three nouns is not one.

whyCorrect: The three items all follow "lay in," so each has to be a gerund phrase: "changing horses," "working through the night," and "taking its turn." Parallel structure requires the third item to match the form of the first two.

whyWrong.A: "the taking of its turn" is a noun phrase rather than a gerund phrase and breaks the pattern.
whyWrong.C: An infinitive does not match the two -ing forms before it.
whyWrong.D: "it took its turn" is a full clause, which cannot sit in a list of gerund phrases governed by "in."

whyCorrect: The subject is "The hand cranes," which is plural; "along the wall of every warehouse on the arm" is a string of prepositional phrases and cannot supply the subject. A plural subject takes "are." Cross out the prepositional phrases and the agreement is obvious.

whyWrong.B: "is" agrees with "arm" or "warehouse," nouns inside prepositional phrases that can never be the subject.
whyWrong.C: "has been" is singular and adds a perfect aspect the sentence does not need.
whyWrong.D: "was" is singular, so it fails agreement whatever its tense.

whyCorrect: There is a stone at every mile, so the positions belong to more than one stone and a plural possessive is needed. A plural already ending in s takes an apostrophe after the s: stones'. The earlier sentence, "reckoned its charges from them," confirms the plural.

whyWrong.A: "stones's" adds a second s to a plural that already ends in one, which Standard English does not do.
whyWrong.C: "stone's" is singular and contradicts the row of mile stones the passage describes.
whyWrong.D: Without an apostrophe the word is a plain plural and "positions" is left with no possessor.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes a legal obligation to release a fixed flow down the old channel every day of the year. The second states what follows for the company: less water available for the summit than the reservoir actually holds. A required daily release logically produces a shortfall, so a result transition is what the sentences call for.

whyWrong.B: "Nevertheless" marks a result that runs against expectation, but this one follows directly.
whyWrong.C: "In contrast" would oppose the two sentences, and the second is the consequence of the first.
whyWrong.D: The shortfall is the general consequence, not one instance of the compensation flow.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says the shafts were sunk to remove spoil and left open only to save the cost of capping. The second says the openings that later vented a tug's smoke were made for a reason unconnected with smoke. That is the same point put a second way, so a restatement transition is right.

whyWrong.A: "Meanwhile" places two things side by side in time, but nothing here happens simultaneously.
whyWrong.C: "By contrast" needs two opposed statements, and these agree.
whyWrong.D: "Nevertheless" concedes something against the first sentence, which the second does not do.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes a boat that carries its crew's home and stops wherever the day ends. The second describes a boat with no cabin, worked between two wharves by men who sleep ashore and never leave a few miles of line. Every detail is the opposite of the first, so the transition must mark a contrast.

whyWrong.A: "Likewise" claims the two are alike, and they are set against each other point by point.
whyWrong.B: "Accordingly" would make the day boat a consequence of the cabin boat, which is not the relationship.
whyWrong.C: "Indeed" intensifies the previous statement, but the second sentence introduces a different type rather than reinforcing the first.

whyCorrect: The goal is the merchant's reason, so the answer needs the rule about duty and the benefit it produced: duty deferred until goods left bond, so a year's stock could be held without finding the money. This choice gives cause and consequence in one sentence. The others describe the warehouse or its costs, which are reasons against rather than for.

whyWrong.B: The Customs lock and the rent are conditions of using a bonded warehouse, not motives for choosing one.
whyWrong.C: Duty on landing is the situation being avoided, stated with no indication of how bond avoids it.
whyWrong.D: Rent and handling are costs the merchant paid, so they cannot explain why he chose the arrangement.

whyCorrect: The audience already knows what a stop lock does, so what needs explaining is why this one falls only four inches. The answer must tie the fall to the four-inch difference in level and state the purpose it serves. Only this choice does both, matching the fall to the difference and naming the water it keeps on the Wenholme side.

whyWrong.A: This defines a stop lock — which the audience knows — and reports the fall without explaining it.
whyWrong.B: The two four-inch figures sit side by side but the choice never says the fall exists because of the difference, nor what it prevents.
whyWrong.C: This gives the purpose without connecting it to the small fall, which is the thing to be explained.

whyCorrect: The goal is what the sale meant for the canal, so the answer must run from the sale to the canal's fate: reservoirs sold in 1902, the canal below left with no supply, closure within a decade. Only this choice carries that consequence. The rest describe the background that made the sale attractive.

whyWrong.A: This explains why the towns wanted the water and says nothing about the canal's fate.
whyWrong.C: Declining traffic and gathered water are the setting, not the outcome of the sale.
whyWrong.D: This states the towns' need and the sale itself, stopping before the effect on the canal.
